rationale: This qualitative study (structured interviews and focus group discussions with 104 purposively sampled women with disabilities plus 7 key informant interviews in three low-income Harare settlements) examines WASH access barriers during the COVID-19 pandemic. The primary rule/governance mechanism analyzed is discretion_accommodation: the failure to implement the National Disability Policy mandate of reasonable accommodation at communal water points, arbitrary and extortionate frontline gatekeeping by community 'borehole marshals' who denied queue priority and demanded cash bribes or transactional sex, and rigid COVID-19 lockdown/curfew and retail sanitiser rules enforced without disability accommodations (with secondary discussion of exclusion from WASH/pandemic planning under participation_assistance and informal water fees/lack of targeted WASH subsidies under fees_tariffs_subsidies). The primary outcome family is effective_access, focusing on physical accessibility of water points, fetching and queueing burdens, water adequacy/quantity for domestic and menstrual hygiene management, and sanitation/hygiene conditions.
